title: Go to the ant
hookLine: go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways (Proverbs 6:6)
carry: steady effort, at the right time

lines: A LINE OF ANTS ON THE COUNTER.
cards: A line of ants crosses a kitchen counter, each one hauling a crumb bigger than its head. One response is a sponge. The book of Proverbs has another: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.”
Not a king, not a sage, not a prophet. The teacher, for once, is tiny, and the student is someone who can't get out of bed. Today: an-Naml.

teach.b: First, meet the sluggard. Proverbs has fun with him. He won't go out, he says, because there's a lion in the street.
And then: “As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.” Turning and turning, going nowhere. The laugh is aimed at a habit, not at a person.

The ant, Proverbs says, works “having no guide, overseer, or ruler.” Nobody stands over her with a clipboard. That's the lesson aimed at the sluggard: not more supervision, but his own reason to get up.

The ant “provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.” She works while the work can be done, so that later there's enough. Some work can't be crammed into the night before.
Later in Proverbs the ants come back, in a list of creatures “little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise.” They are “a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer.”
Wisdom here isn't size or strength. It's steady effort, at the right time, with nobody watching. The ant has a neighbor's echo, too: in the Qur'an, a surah is named for the ant, an-Naml.
In it, an ant calls to the others to get out of the way of Solomon's army, and Solomon smiles at her words.

how: Some Jewish and Christian teachers use Proverbs 6:6 to teach diligence, sometimes alongside the lazy man of Proverbs 26, and the Qur'an names a surah for the ant.

games.q: you're the sluggard, and Proverbs sends you to learn from a teacher. who?
games.why: “go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.” the smallest teacher in the room.

practice: Find something small at work nearby, ants on a path, a bird carrying a twig, rain filling a gutter, the second hand of a clock, or bring one to mind, and watch it without hurrying it: the small motion, repeated, steady, waiting for no one's permission.
Let your breath settle to its pace, and let one small piece of your own work come to mind, before the season for it passes. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: An-Naml. The Qur'an's surah named for the ant, where an ant calls others out of Solomon's army's way. Today's word.
